Rocky Hill Police Department 
"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
 
Brian P. Klett 
Chief of Police 
 
 
ROCKY HILL POLICE DEPARTMENT 
GENERAL ORDER 
CHAPTER  61 
NUMBER 
61-1 (a) 
TITLE: AUTOMATIC LICENSE PLATE READERS (ALPR) 
EFFECTIVE: 08/5/14 ISSUED: B.P.K. REVIEW:  
REVISED: 10/1/26 
RESCINDS:  
CALEA REFERENCE: 41.3.9 
STATE REFERENCE:  
 
PURPOSE 
 
The purpose of this policy is to establish requirements and safeguards governing the 
operation and use of Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) systems and access 
to ALPR data by the Rocky Hill Police Department. 
 
This policy establishes standards for ALPR system operation, data collection, access, 
querying, sharing, retention, security, auditing, training, vendor management, 
transparency, and accountability. 
 
The Department recognizes that ALPR technology can assist legitimate law 
enforcement and public safety functions while also creating significant privacy and civil-
liberty concerns because the technology may collect information concerning vehicles 
traveling in public places. 
 
ALPR technology shall therefore be used only for authorized purposes and in 
accordance with applicable federal law, Connecticut law, applicable regulations, the 
current Connecticut Police Officer Standards and Training Council (POSTC) Model 
Policy, and this Department policy.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
POLICY 
 
It is the policy of the Rocky Hill Police Department to use ALPR technology only for 
legitimate law enforcement and authorized public safety purposes. 
 
ALPR systems and ALPR data shall not be used for personal purposes, harassment, 
intimidation, retaliation, discrimination, investigation of constitutionally protected activity, 
prohibited immigration enforcement, prohibited investigations involving lawful 
reproductive or gender-affirming health care, or any other purpose prohibited by 
Connecticut or federal law. 
 
All personnel authorized to use ALPR technology shall comply with this policy and shall 
complete required initial and periodic training before obtaining or continuing access. 
 
ALPR OVERVIEW 
 
ALPR technology uses cameras and software to capture images of vehicle license 
plates and, depending upon the system, vehicle characteristics such as make, model, 
color, and other identifying information. 
 
The system may convert captured information into computer-readable data and 
compare that information against authorized databases or lists. 
 
ALPR technology may assist with authorized purposes including: 
 
• Identifying stolen or wanted vehicles; 
 
• Identifying stolen license plates; 
 
• Locating missing or endangered persons; 
 
• Locating persons with outstanding warrants; 
 
• Recovering stolen property or stolen vehicles; 
 
• Assisting specific active criminal investigations; 
 
• Assisting in circumstances involving flight or evasion from law 
enforcement; 
 
• Responding to emergencies; 
 
• Identifying vehicles associated with authorized alerts or databases; and 
 
• Other purposes expressly permitted by Connecticut law.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
An ALPR alert is not, standing alone, conclusive evidence that a vehicle, license plate, 
or person is wanted or otherwise involved in criminal activity. 
 
DEFINITIONS 
 
a. ALPR: Automated License Recognition, also referred to as Automated  
License Plate Reader. 
 
b. ALPR Administrator: The person designated by the Chief of Police to  
oversee the Department's ALPR program, including compliance, access, 
training, security, auditing, system management, reporting, and policy 
implementation. 
 
c. ALPR Data: Data generated by or obtained through an ALPR system,  
including captured license plate information, images, vehicle descriptors, 
location information, timestamps, metadata, alert information, scan files, and 
associated records, as defined by applicable law. 
 
d. Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) device: consists of cameras 
enclosed in housings connected to a computer system whether hardwired or 
cloud-based that is designed to automatically recognize and interpret the 
characters on vehicle license plates.  A LPR may be fixed or mobile (mounted 
on a vehicle or trailer). 
 
e. ALPR Operator: A trained Department member or other authorized person  
permitted to operate an ALPR system. 
 
f. ALPR System: ALPR cameras and associated hardware, software, 
databases, networks, and related technology used by the Department, 
including fixed and mobile systems. 
 
g. Alert/Hit: A visual, electronic, and/or auditory notification indicating that ALPR 
 data may correspond to information contained in an authorized list or 
database. 
An alert does not establish that the information is current or that the vehicle is 
the vehicle associated with the underlying record. 
 
h. Gender-Affirming Health Care Services: As defined in Conn. Gen. Statute 
52-571m. 
 
i. Hot List: A list of license plate numbers or other vehicle identifiers maintained  
for an authorized law enforcement purpose and used to generate ALPR 
alerts. 
 
j. Internal Hotlist Addendum: A hotlist that (A) is maintained for use only at 
specific state facility or facilities for which the list was made and by the public

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
agency that made such list, and (B) may contain registration numbers 
displayed on a license plate of a motor vehicle registered to a person who is 
identified in the making of such list as a potential threat to a person in the 
state facility, to the state facility or against the public agency operating the 
state facility, for reasons that include a previous conviction of such person for 
a misdemeanor or felony offense involving threats of physical violence or 
harassment against a person in the state facility, to the state facility or against 
the public agency operating the state facility or conduct by a person that is 
documented and involves threats of or attempted violence, harassment or 
incitement of physical violence against a person in the state facility, to the 
state facility or against the public agency operating the state facility, provided 
no such inclusion on an internal Hotlist addendum is based on an arrest for or 
conduct that is solely speech, conduct or association protected by article first 
of the Constitution of the state or the first amendment to the United States 
Constitution. 
 
k. Reproductive Health Care Services: As defined in Conn. Gen. Stat. 52a-
571m.   
 
l. LPR Notification: A message generated by an LPR system which notifies 
the user that a vehicle is a potential match for a list, whether locally 
generated, created by neighboring jurisdictions, or based on NCIC records.  
An LPR notification does not represent conclusive confirmation that the 
information contained in the notification is accurate.  Sometimes referred to 
as a “hit”. 
 
m. Query: A search of ALPR data using specified criteria, including a license 
plate number, vehicle characteristics, date, time, location, or other authorized 
parameters. 
 
n. Query Log: A record of an ALPR data search or query, including information 
required by law or Department policy. 
 
o. State Facility: As defined by the applicable POSTC Model Policy and 
Connecticut Law. 
 
 
This policy applies to any equipment, service, platform, or network that performs 
ALPR functions or provides the Department access to ALPR data, regardless of 
vendor or ownership. 
 
ALPR ADMINISTRATOR 
 
The Chief of Police shall designate an ALPR Administrator. 
 
The ALPR Administrator shall:

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
 
1. Ensure the ALPR system is used only for authorized Department business; 
 
2. Ensure compliance with applicable federal and Connecticut law, the current 
POSTC Model Policy, and this policy; 
 
3. Authorize and manage user access; 
 
4. Issue or approve user credentials; 
 
5. Ensure required initial and periodic training is completed; 
 
6. Monitor system security and privacy safeguards; 
 
7. Monitor system operation and coordinate repairs; 
 
8. Review or coordinate review of requests for external sharing of ALPR data; 
 
9. Conduct, or cause to be conducted, ALPR audits at least monthly; 
 
10. Review system access and query logs; 
 
11. Review ALPR data retention activity, including the number of times data is 
retained beyond the ordinary retention period and the duration of such 
retention; 
 
12. Ensure audit deficiencies are documented and corrective action is taken; 
 
13. Maintain records required by law and Department policy; 
 
14. Ensure required annual ALPR usage reports are prepared and submitted; 
 
15. Ensure required transparency information is published; 
 
16. Identify and report policy or legal violations to the Chief of Police; 
 
17. Recommend necessary policy, training, or system changes; and 
 
18. Ensure changes in law, regulation, POSTC requirements, DESPP 
requirements, or ALPR technology are incorporated into Department 
procedures and training.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
AUTHORIZED USE 
 
ALPR systems and ALPR data may be operated, accessed, queried, or used only for 
purposes authorized by Connecticut law and this policy. 
 
Authorized law enforcement uses include, when applicable legal requirements are 
satisfied: 
 
a. Comparing ALPR information with an authorized hot list; 
 
b. Comparing information with authorized Connecticut criminal justice 
databases; 
 
c. Using ALPR data in connection with a specific active criminal investigation 
when reasonable suspicion exists that a criminal offense has been or is being 
committed and the required documentation is completed; 
 
d. Assisting in the apprehension of an individual with an outstanding warrant; 
 
e. Assisting in locating a missing or endangered individual; 
 
f. Assisting in the recovery of a stolen motor vehicle; 
 
g. Responding to circumstances otherwise authorized by Connecticut law; 
 
h. Using authorized state, federal, or national databases where the use is 
permitted by law and applicable policy; and 
 
i. Other purposes expressly authorized by Connecticut law. 
 
The Department shall not use ALPR data merely because a person or vehicle is of 
general interest to law enforcement. 
 
For a specific criminal investigation, personnel shall document the factual basis for 
accessing the data and the associated case, complaint, or incident number as required 
by law. 
 
When a case, complaint, or incident number exists, the query shall be linked to an 
independently verifiable Department record when practicable. 
 
QUERIES AND ACCESS 
 
An authorized user shall: 
 
1. Log into the ALPR system using individually assigned credentials;

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
2. Use the system only for an authorized purpose; 
 
3. Enter only the parameters necessary to conduct the authorized query; 
 
4. Document the reason for the query; 
 
5. Identify the applicable offense or authorized purpose when required; 
 
6. Enter the applicable case, complaint, incident, or other identifying number 
when required; 
 
7. Complete any additional CAD or report documentation required by this policy. 
 
 
Queries shall comply with any applicable reasonable-suspicion, probable-cause, 
warrant, or other legal requirement. 
 
Exigent access shall be identified at the time of access, justified in writing with a call for 
service number and case report, and included in a supervisory review. 
 
Users shall not conduct queries merely out of curiosity or for personal purposes. 
 
DEPARTMENT CASE QUERIES 
 
When an officer searches or conducts a query for an ALPR-related purpose involving a 
Rocky Hill Police Department case, the officer shall document the reason for the query 
in the original case report whenever practicable. 
 
If the original report has already been completed, the officer shall complete a 
supplemental report to the original case documenting: 
 
• The date and time of the query; 
 
• The officer conducting the query; 
 
• The case or incident number; 
 
• The information or vehicle searched, when appropriate; 
 
• The reason and authorized law enforcement purpose for the query; and 
 
• Any relevant information obtained as a result of the query. 
 
The documentation requirement applies regardless of whether the query produces 
information of investigative value.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
HOT LISTS 
 
Authorized users may enter license plate numbers or other vehicle identifiers into an 
authorized hot list only for a legitimate purpose permitted by law and this policy. 
 
Before a manual hot-list entry is created: 
 
1. The entry shall be approved by an authorized supervisor when required; 
 
2. The offense or authorized purpose shall be documented; 
 
3. The vehicle description and officer information shall be documented when 
applicable; 
 
4. The entry shall have an appropriate expiration date; 
 
5. The license plate information shall be verified through appropriate law 
enforcement databases when practicable; and 
 
6. The entry shall be removed when the expiration period ends or when the 
underlying purpose no longer exists. 
 
Hot-list entries shall not be based solely upon constitutionally protected speech, 
association, assembly, petitioning activity, or other protected conduct.  Hot lists received 
from outside sources shall identify the source and be periodically verified and updated 
prior to being re-entered.   
 
BOLO AND ALERT ENTRY PROCEDURES 
 
A. BOLO’s Received by Dispatch From Outside Agencies 
 
When the Rocky Hill Police Department receives a BOLO or other ALPR-related 
request from an outside law enforcement agency or other authorized outside agency 
and dispatch is requested or directed to enter the information into the Department's 
ALPR system: 
 
• The dispatcher shall obtain approval from the Shift Commander before 
entering the BOLO into the ALPR system; 
 
• The dispatcher shall create a call for service number (CFS) in CAD under the 
REKOR ENTRY call type. 
 
• The CAD entry shall identify the source of the BOLO and provide sufficient 
information to identify the vehicle, license plate, or other subject of the alert. 
 
•   The dispatcher shall document the Shift Commander's approval.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
 
• When the underlying BOLO or request expires, is cancelled, or is otherwise 
no longer valid, the Department shall take reasonable steps to remove or 
deactivate the corresponding ALPR alert. 
 
B. Officer-Initiated ALPR Entries Not Associated With a RHPD Call for Service 
 
When a Rocky Hill Police Department officer determines that an ALPR entry is 
necessary and the entry is not associated with an existing call for service number in 
the Town of Rocky Hill.   
 
• The officer shall obtain approval from the Shift Commander before making the 
entry.   
 
• Obtain a call for service number under REKOR ENTRY call type; and  
 
• Then document the purpose of the entry in a police report.   
 
• When practical a CAD entry should also be made to detail the reason for the 
department alert. 
 
 
C. Department Alerts Associated With Rocky Hill Calls for Service 
 
When a Department ALPR alert is associated with an existing call for service in the 
Town of Rocky Hill, the officer shall obtain Shift Commander approval before 
creating or activating the Department alert.  The officer shall document the alert 
entry in a case or supplemental report associated with the call for service. 
 
 
ALPR ALERTS AND TRAFFIC STOPS 
 
An ALPR alert shall not, by itself, establish reasonable suspicion or probable cause. 
 
Before taking enforcement action based upon an ALPR alert, when circumstances 
permit, officers shall: 
 
• Visually verify that the license plate and other identifying characteristics 
correspond to the alert; 
• Confirm the status of the underlying record through COLLECT, NCIC, 
RMS, or another appropriate source; 
• Confirm, when practicable, that the underlying record remains active; and 
• Develop independent reasonable suspicion, probable cause, or other 
legally sufficient grounds for the enforcement action. 
• Consider the totality of the circumstances.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
Before proceeding with additional law enforcement action based on an ALPR hit, 
officers shall receive confirmation from communications or other authorized personnel 
that the hit remains active, unless exigent circumstances exist. 
 
PROHIBITED USES 
 
ALPR systems and data shall not be used: 
 
• For personal purposes; 
 
• To harass, intimidate, retaliate against, or target an individual or group; 
 
• To monitor or investigate an individual based on actual or perceived race, 
ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, sex, pregnancy 
status, disability, citizenship, nationality, income level, or perceived criminal 
history, except when a prior conviction is an element of the offense being 
investigated; 
 
• To identify, monitor, investigate, or impose liability upon a person solely for 
constitutionally protected speech, assembly, association, petitioning, or other 
First Amendment activity; 
 
• To investigate suspected immigration violations or otherwise assist in civil or 
criminal immigration enforcement, except where expressly authorized by 
controlling law; 
 
• To investigate or prosecute an individual for seeking, receiving, providing, or 
assisting another person in obtaining reproductive health care services or 
gender-affirming health care services that are legal in Connecticut, or in any 
manner that would violate Conn. Gen. Stat. 54-155b. 
 
• To circumvent Connecticut restrictions concerning public resources or law 
enforcement activities; 
 
• To obtain information for a purpose unrelated to an authorized ALPR use; 
 
• To provide unauthorized access to ALPR data; or 
 
• For any other purpose prohibited by federal or Connecticut law. 
 
DEPARTMENT & POST DISCIPLINARY ACTION  
 
If a law enforcement officer is found to have knowingly accessed, used, or disseminated 
ALPR data with malicious intent for purposes beyond the act’s allowable uses, the 
ALPR Administrator shall notify POSTC of suspected malicious misuse.  The officer is 
subject to disciplinary action up to and including termination.  The officer may also be

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
subjected to POST disciplinary action, such as suspension, cancellation, or revocation 
of his or her POST certification. 
 
DEPLOYMENT STANDARDS 
 
Before installation, each fixed ALPR device shall have written justification identifying the 
deployment category, location-based rationale, data relied upon, and material 
limitations.  The justification shall be retained for the life of the deployment.  Deployment 
categories are gateway, corridor, targeted, and asset protection.  Deployment reviews 
shall consider travel-path exposure, not device count alone.  Targeted deployments 
shall have a defined review or sunset date and require written re-justification for 
continuation. 
 
The Department shall maintain an established baseline for fixed ALPR deployments.  
Expansion beyond the baseline shall be presented to the municipal legislative body, 
police commission, or other designated committee, as applicable.  Fixed ALPR 
locations shall be publicly posted when permitted by law. 
 
COLLECTION RESTRICTIONS 
 
The Department shall comply with all Connecticut statutory restrictions concerning 
collection of ALPR data at or near protected facilities and organizations. 
 
Unless authorized pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. 29-6d, the Department shall not collect

Description

Every successful AMBER plan contains clearly defined activation criteria. The following guidance is designed to achieve a uniform, interoperable network of plans across the country, and to minimize potentially deadly delays because of confusion among varying jurisdictions.

Flowchart: What Happens When Law Enforcement Issues an AMBER Alert (View larger image.)

National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (see reuse policy).

## Summary of Department of Justice Recommended Criteria

* There is reasonable belief by law enforcement that an abduction has occurred.
* The law enforcement agency believes that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.
* There is enough descriptive information about the victim and the abduction for law enforcement to issue an AMBER Alert to assist in the recovery of the child.
* The abduction is of a child aged 17 years or younger.
* The child’s name and other critical data elements, including the Child Abduction flag, have been entered into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) system.

### There is reasonable belief by law enforcement that an abduction has occurred.

AMBER plans require law enforcement to confirm an abduction prior to issuing an alert. This is essential when determining the level of risk to the child. Clearly, stranger abductions are the most dangerous for children and thus are primary to the mission of an AMBER Alert. To allow activations in the absence of significant information that an abduction has occurred could lead to abuse of the system and ultimately weaken its effectiveness. At the same time, each case must be appraised on its own merits and a judgment call made quickly. Law enforcement must understand that a “best judgment” approach, based on the evidence, is appropriate and necessary.

### The law enforcement agency believes that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.

Plans require a child be at risk for serious bodily harm or death before an alert can be issued. This element is clearly related to law enforcement’s recognition that stranger abductions represent the greatest danger to children. The need for timely, accurate information based on strict and clearly understood criteria is critical, again keeping in mind the “best judgment” approach.

### There is enough descriptive information about the victim and the abduction for law enforcement to issue an AMBER Alert to assist in the recovery of the child.

For an AMBER Alert to be effective in recovering a missing child, the law enforcement agency must have enough information to believe that an immediate broadcast to the public will enhance the efforts of law enforcement to locate the child and apprehend the suspect. This element requires as much descriptive information as possible about the abducted child and the abduction, as well as descriptive information about the suspect and the suspect’s vehicle. Issuing alerts in the absence of significant information that an abduction has occurred could lead to abuse of the system and ultimately weaken its effectiveness.

### The abduction is of a child aged 17 years or younger.

Every state adopt the “17 years of age or younger” standard; or, at a minimum, agree to honor the request of any other state to issue an AMBER Alert, even if the case does not meet the responding state’s age criterion, as long as it meets the age criterion of the requesting state. Most AMBER plans call for activation of the alert for children under a certain age. The problem is that age can vary—some plans specify 10, some 12, some 14, 15, and 16. Differences in age requirements create confusion when an activation requires multiple alerts across states and jurisdictions. Overuse of the AMBER Alert system will undermine its effectiveness as a tool for recovering abducted children.

### The child's name and other critical data elements, including the Child Abduction flag, have been entered into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) system.

Immediately enter AMBER Alert data into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) system. Text information describing the circumstances surrounding the abduction of the child should be entered, and the case flagged as a Child Abduction. Many plans do not mandate entry of the data into NCIC, but this omission undermines the entire mission of the AMBER Alert initiative. The notation on the entry should be sufficient to explain the circumstances of the disappearance of the child. Entry of the alert data into NCIC expands the search for an abducted child from the local, state, or regional level to the national. This is a critical element of any effective AMBER Alert plan.

## Overview

AMBER Alerts are activated in the most serious child-abduction cases. The goal of an AMBER Alert is to instantly galvanize the community to assist in the search for and safe recovery of a missing child.  These alerts are broadcast through radio, TV, road signs, cellphones, and other data-enabled devices. The AMBER Alert system is being used in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, Indian country, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and 27 other countries.

The U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Justice Programs has tasked the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children with managing the AMBER Alert Secondary Distribution Program. When law enforcement issues an AMBER Alert, NCMEC is notified and re-distributes the alert to the appropriate secondary distributors.

**As of December 31, 2025: 1,313 children have been recovered due to the activation of an AMBER Alert. Of those, at least 253 are due to the use of a Wireless Emergency Alert (WEA) message.**

## How do I receive AMBER Alerts?

AMBER Alerts are broadcast through radio, television, road signs, and the network of secondary distributors, which include digital signage, hotel chains, internet service providers, apps, and other technology.  As of 2013, AMBER Alerts are also delivered to wireless phones through the Wireless Emergency Alerts program (WEA).

Most people will see AMBER Alerts directly from primary distribution and secondary distributors and do not require any additional steps. You may also be notified of an AMBER Alert in the following ways:

**On Facebook:**Visit www.facebook.com/AMBERAlert and “Like” the page to receive AMBER Alerts in your newsfeed. Facebook also automatically notifies users near the location of an AMBER Alert.

**On Instagram:**  If an AMBER Alert is activated by law enforcement and you are in the designated search area, the alert will appear in your Instagram feed.

**On Twitter:** Follow @AMBERAlert to receive rapid AMBER Alert notifications on your Twitter feed and share the alert with your followers.

Countries around the world followed the success of AMBER Alerts in the U.S. and created similar rapid alert systems. **What happens when an AMBER Alert is received?**

o   AMBER Alert broadcasts have a unique audible signal and vibration. It is intended to indicate the urgency of the message and make the alert accessible to people with hearing or vision-related disabilities. The message will contain a limited number of characters and provide basic information.

o   In the case of an AMBER Alert, the message would indicate that an AMBER Alert has been issued for your area and, relevant information about the missing child, and if possible, the abductor and/or vehicle used in the abduction.

**How do AMBER Alerts work?**

o   Once law enforcement has been notified about an abducted child, they will decide whether or not to issue an AMBER Alert based on their AMBER Alert program's criteria. They will provide the geographic area where the alert should be issued as well as any available information about the child, abductor, or suspected vehicle used in the abduction.

o   Once issued, the alerts are distributed by broadcasters and transportation agencies. They are also sent to NCMEC which redistribute the alerts to a network of secondary distributors that includes internet service providers, digital billboards, truckers, and others.

**How are AMBER Alerts distributed to cell phones?**

o   AMBER Alerts are distributed to cell phones as part of the AMBER Alert program's secondary distribution through the Wireless Emergency Alert program (WEA).

**What is the Wireless Emergency Alert program?**

o   The Wireless Emergency Alert program is operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. It distributes notifications from authorized federal, state, local, and tribal government agencies that alert customers with capable devices of imminent threats to safety or an emergency situation. The messages are intended as a supplement to the existing Emergency Alert System, which broadcasts alerts over radio and television.

o   In addition to AMBER Alerts, the program includes National Weather Service, Presidential, and imminent threat alerts. If you own a capable mobile device, you will automatically receive these alerts when you are in the geographic area where an alert has been issued.

o   Because the alerts are sent on a special wireless carrier channel called Cell Broadcast they are not affected by congestion on the voice or SMS text channels. The alerts are transmitted simultaneously to all mobile devices within range of the cellular carrier towers in the affected area. # AMBER Alert Plan

## California AMBER Alert Plan

The California AMBER Alert Plan is a voluntary partnership between law enforcement, transportation, and media to rapidly disseminate information about a suspect and victim to law enforcement agencies and the public when a child has been abducted. California's AMBER Alert Plan has been part of the state's comprehensive child recovery strategy since it was launched in August, 2002.

## Key Partners

The California Broadcasters Association, California Department of Transportation, National Weather Service, California Lottery, GTECH, Facebook, X, Instagram, Nixle, California law enforcement agencies, and the media.

## Activation Process

California AMBER Alerts are initiated solely by California law enforcement agencies. Law enforcement agencies must follow strict activation criteria before an alert is activated. The agency's administration must give approval before initiating an AMBER Alert. The primary consideration in the development of the activation criteria was the identification of those abducted children who are at the greatest risk of serious bodily injury or death.

In order for the California AMBER Alert Plan to be activated, law enforcement must be satisfied the following criteria have been met:

* It has been confirmed that an abduction has occurred, or the child has been taken by anybody including, but not limited to, parents and/or guardians.
* The victim is 17 years of age or younger, or of proven mental or physical disability.
* There is reason to believe the victim is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.
* There is information available that, if disseminated to the general public, could assist in the safe recovery of the victim.

The AMBER Alert cannot be used for custodial disputes or runaway cases that don't meet the criteria. Law enforcement agencies are encouraged to issue an Endangered Missing Advisories for cases that don't meet the criteria. Here are the steps a law enforcement agency must take once it has been determined that the criteria have been met:

* If the agency is within a CARE county (Los Angeles, Orange, Alameda, or San Diego) contact the local Sheriff's Department.
* If the agency is not within a CARE county, contact the California Highway Patrol.
* The agency should set up a phone "hotline" to handle tips and appoint a public information officer to handle the press.
* The agency should obtain current photos of the victim and if possible the suspect.

## Distribution Process

The California Highway Patrol will distribute AMBER Alerts to law enforcement, broadcasters, National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), Lottery, Ports of Entry, and members of the public who have registered to receive the alerts. Those alerts will be sent to computers, cell phones and text messaging devices.

* CHP will use the Emergency Alert System (EAS) to initially notify California broadcasters of the alert.
* CHP will also post the alert on its website www.chp.ca.gov.
* CHP will send out flyers to law enforcement agencies and businesses throughout California and surrounding states.
* California Department of Transportation will distribute the alerts on Changeable Message Signs (CMS).
* Media outlets will also post alerts on their websites.
* NCMEC will disseminate the alerts through secondary distributors, i.e. Internet providers, Facebook, trucking associations, airport security, X, Nixle, etc.
* Numerous private businesses have agreed to put the alerts on their electronic signs.

## APBnet

APBnet is a web-based system that captures and immediately distributes color photographs and images to law enforcement agencies, media outlets, and other organizations. In addition, the system is capable of transmitting information via facsimile to business, hospitals, schools, media outlets, and agencies. The APBnet system can be used to quickly disseminate information regarding a child abduction case throughout the state.

When the CHP receives word of a confirmed child abduction which meets the AMBER Alert criteria, it can post Critical Reach flyers, photographs and other pertinent information on the department's Computer Aided Dispatch (CAD)/media Web site (cad.chp.ca.gov) and public Web site (www.chp.ca.gov).

## Wireless Emergency Alerts Program (WEA)

The Wireless Emergency Alerts will allow consumers with WEA-capable smartphones and feature phones to automatically receive free AMBER Alert messages, along with Presidential and Imminent Threat Alerts. When a subscriber with a WEA enabled cellular phone is within range of the activated cell tower they will receive the AMBER Alerts, even if the wireless customer is not from the area. The program is an "opt out" program, meaning subscribers do not have to enroll in the program to receive alerts. The WEA AMBER Alert notification is automatically sent from National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) at the time of the AMBER Alert activation. The message includes an audible tone followed by a text-like message.

## Changeable Message Signs

The Changeable Message Signs will contain the following message when the suspect's vehicle information is known:

* CHILD ABDUCTION
* VEHICLE DESCRIPTION
* LICENSE PLATE NUMBER

## Law Enforcement Responsibilities

* Each agency should have an established protocol to govern their use of the AMBER Alert Plan within the agency's child recovery plan.
* All law enforcement personnel should be trained on the AMBER Alert criteria and notification process.
* Each agency agrees to designate correct personnel who have the authority to issue the AMBER Alert.
* Each agency agrees to abide by the established criteria and activation procedure and all other components of the plan.
* Each agency agrees to respond to any questions or concerns raised by the AMBER Alert Advisory Committee.

## Media Responsibilities

* Each media outlet should have an established protocol to govern the receipt and broadcast of an AMBER Alert.
* Each media outlet should train all employees on the AMBER Alert criteria and the steps to follow to broadcast the alert.
* Each media outlet should post the AMBER Alert on their web sites.
* Each media outlet should help educate the public about the AMBER Alert through news stories, public service announcements and participating in AMBER Alert tests.

## Training

The training for law enforcement and broadcasters must provide instruction on all aspects of the state's plan, including its activation criteria and broadcasting procedures.

* CHP will provide training to law enforcement agencies and communications centers on criteria and activation procedures.
* The AMBER Alert Coordinator will keep current on training and other resources to assist all members of the team to make sure the plan is working effectively.
* The AMBER Alert Coordinator will help write and produce protocols and training materials.

## Community Awareness

The AMBER Alert Coordinator will work with the Broadcaster's Association to make sure citizens of California are familiar with the AMBER Alert Plan in order to enhance its success in the safe recovery of abducted children. The public information campaign will let the public know how the AMBER Alert Plan works and how to help in the safe recovery an abducted child. A public information campaign will include public service announcements, public awareness events and written materials.

The California AMBER Alert Advisory Committee will also seek out businesses and private individuals to help in the implementation of the California AMBER Alert Plan. Employers will be encouraged to notify all of their employees of AMBER Alerts. Private businesses with electronic signs, Internet providers, websites and other means to communicate with the public will be encouraged to offer AMBER Alert notifications.

Description

Every successful AMBER plan contains clearly defined activation criteria. The following guidance is designed to achieve a uniform, interoperable network of plans across the country, and to minimize potentially deadly delays because of confusion among varying jurisdictions.

Flowchart: What Happens When Law Enforcement Issues an AMBER Alert (View larger image.)

## Summary of Department of Justice Recommended Criteria

* There is reasonable belief by law enforcement that an abduction has occurred.
* The law enforcement agency believes that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.
* There is enough descriptive information about the victim and the abduction for law enforcement to issue an AMBER Alert to assist in the recovery of the child.
* The abduction is of a child aged 17 years or younger.
* The child’s name and other critical data elements, including the Child Abduction flag, have been entered into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) system.

### There is reasonable belief by law enforcement that an abduction has occurred.

AMBER plans require law enforcement to confirm an abduction prior to issuing an alert. This is essential when determining the level of risk to the child. Clearly, stranger abductions are the most dangerous for children and thus are primary to the mission of an AMBER Alert. To allow activations in the absence of significant information that an abduction has occurred could lead to abuse of the system and ultimately weaken its effectiveness. At the same time, each case must be appraised on its own merits and a judgment call made quickly. Law enforcement must understand that a “best judgment” approach, based on the evidence, is appropriate and necessary.

### The law enforcement agency believes that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury or death.

Plans require a child be at risk for serious bodily harm or death before an alert can be issued. This element is clearly related to law enforcement’s recognition that stranger abductions represent the greatest danger to children. The need for timely, accurate information based on strict and clearly understood criteria is critical, again keeping in mind the “best judgment” approach.

### There is enough descriptive information about the victim and the abduction for law enforcement to issue an AMBER Alert to assist in the recovery of the child.

For an AMBER Alert to be effective in recovering a missing child, the law enforcement agency must have enough information to believe that an immediate broadcast to the public will enhance the efforts of law enforcement to locate the child and apprehend the suspect. This element requires as much descriptive information as possible about the abducted child and the abduction, as well as descriptive information about the suspect and the suspect’s vehicle. Issuing alerts in the absence of significant information that an abduction has occurred could lead to abuse of the system and ultimately weaken its effectiveness.

### The abduction is of a child aged 17 years or younger.

GENERAL ORDER

TITLE: AUTOMATIC LICENSE PLATE READERS (ALPR)

PURPOSE 
 
The purpose of this policy is to establish requirements and safeguards governing the 
operation and use of Automated License Plate Recognition (ALPR) systems and access 
to ALPR data by the Rocky Hill Police Department. 
 
This policy establishes standards for ALPR system operation, data collection, access, 
querying, sharing, retention, security, auditing, training, vendor management, 
transparency, and accountability. 
 
The Department recognizes that ALPR technology can assist legitimate law 
enforcement and public safety functions while also creating significant privacy and civil-
liberty concerns because the technology may collect information concerning vehicles 
traveling in public places. 
 
ALPR technology shall therefore be used only for authorized purposes and in 
accordance with applicable federal law, Connecticut law, applicable regulations, the 
current Connecticut Police Officer Standards and Training Council (POSTC) Model 
Policy, and this Department policy.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
POLICY 
 
It is the policy of the Rocky Hill Police Department to use ALPR technology only for 
legitimate law enforcement and authorized public safety purposes. 
 
ALPR systems and ALPR data shall not be used for personal purposes, harassment, 
intimidation, retaliation, discrimination, investigation of constitutionally protected activity, 
prohibited immigration enforcement, prohibited investigations involving lawful 
reproductive or gender-affirming health care, or any other purpose prohibited by 
Connecticut or federal law. 
 
All personnel authorized to use ALPR technology shall comply with this policy and shall 
complete required initial and periodic training before obtaining or continuing access. 
 
ALPR OVERVIEW 
 
ALPR technology uses cameras and software to capture images of vehicle license 
plates and, depending upon the system, vehicle characteristics such as make, model, 
color, and other identifying information. 
 
The system may convert captured information into computer-readable data and 
compare that information against authorized databases or lists. 
 
ALPR technology may assist with authorized purposes including: 
 
• Identifying stolen or wanted vehicles; 
 
• Identifying stolen license plates; 
 
• Locating missing or endangered persons; 
 
• Locating persons with outstanding warrants; 
 
• Recovering stolen property or stolen vehicles; 
 
• Assisting specific active criminal investigations; 
 
• Assisting in circumstances involving flight or evasion from law 
enforcement; 
 
• Responding to emergencies; 
 
• Identifying vehicles associated with authorized alerts or databases; and 
 
• Other purposes expressly permitted by Connecticut law.

"A Police-Community Partnership Since 1938" 
An ALPR alert is not, standing alone, conclusive evidence that a vehicle, license plate, 
or person is wanted or otherwise involved in criminal activity. 
 
DEFINITIONS 
 
a. ALPR: Automated License Recognition, also referred to as Automated  
License Plate Reader.

The California AMBER Alert Plan is a voluntary partnership between law enforcement, transportation, and media to rapidly disseminate information about a suspect and victim to law enforcement agencies and the public when a child has been abducted.
